legend.meaning: coordinates of a point on the terminal side

explanation: Let $ \theta $ be an angle in standard position, and let $ (x, y) $ be a point on its terminal side, at a distance $ r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} $ from the origin.
The [[kw:general definitions]] of the six trigonometric functions are:
$$ \sin \theta = \frac{y}{r} \quad \csc \theta = \frac{r}{y} \, (y \neq 0) $$
$$ \cos \theta = \frac{x}{r} \quad \sec \theta = \frac{r}{x} \, (x \neq 0) $$
$$ \tan \theta = \frac{y}{x} \, (x \neq 0) \quad \cot \theta = \frac{x}{y} \, (y \neq 0) $$
The signs of the functions depend on the quadrant in which the terminal side lies. The radius $ r $ is always positive.

discoveryHook.scenario: Right triangle definitions only work for acute angles. But what if the angle is 150° or even -60°? By placing the angle in a circle and using coordinates, we can define the six trigonometric functions for [[imp:any angle]]—opening up the full power of trigonometry.

confusionCorner.title: Radius Is Always Positive
confusionCorner.body: The distance $ r $ is the length of the hypotenuse of the reference right triangle, so it is [[imp:always positive]]. The signs of the trigonometric functions come only from the signs of $ x $ and $ y $.

blocks.title: The Unit Circle and Quadrantal Angles

confusionCorner.title: Undefined vs. Zero
confusionCorner.body: When the terminal side is on an axis, some trigonometric functions are zero, and others are [[imp:undefined]] because their definitions involve division by zero. For example, at 180°, $ \sin \theta = 0 $ but $ \csc \theta $ is undefined. Don't confuse the two!

teacherCues: Draw the unit circle $ x^2 + y^2 = 1 $. Ask: Why does $ \sin \theta = y $ and $ \cos \theta = x $ on the unit circle?
Ask: What are the coordinates of the points where the terminal side of $ 90^\circ $, $ 180^\circ $, $ 270^\circ $ intersect the unit circle? How can we use them to find trigonometric values?

explanation: The [[kw:unit circle]] is the circle $ x^2 + y^2 = 1 $ centered at the origin. Because $ r = 1 $, the definitions simplify to $ \sin \theta = y $ and $ \cos \theta = x $.
A [[kw:quadrantal angle]] is an angle in standard position whose terminal side lies on an axis. Its measure is a multiple of $ 90^\circ $ or $ \frac{\pi}{2} $ radians.
For quadrantal angles, the coordinates are: $ 0^\circ $: $ (1,0) $; $ 90^\circ $: $ (0,1) $; $ 180^\circ $: $ (-1,0) $; $ 270^\circ $: $ (0,-1) $.
Using these coordinates, you can directly read $ \sin \theta $ and $ \cos \theta $ and compute the other four functions. Some will be undefined where a coordinate is zero (division by zero).
For angles that are coterminal with quadrantal angles, such as $ 540^\circ $ (coterminal with $ 180^\circ $), use the same coordinates.

examples.prompt: Use the unit circle to evaluate the six trigonometric functions of $ \theta = 270^\circ $.
examples.title: Example A — Evaluate at 270°
steps: The terminal side intersects the unit circle at $ (0, -1) $. So $ x = 0, y = -1, r = 1 $.
At 90°, the point on the unit circle is $ (0, 1) $.
Division by zero is undefined, so $ \tan 90^\circ $ does not exist.
This is why the tangent function has vertical asymptotes at odd multiples of 90°.

discoveryHook.scenario: The unit circle—a circle with radius 1—is the ultimate tool for trigonometry. Because $ r = 1 $, the sine and cosine of any angle are simply the $ y $- and $ x $-coordinates of the point where the terminal side meets the circle. Quadrantal angles (0°, 90°, 180°, 270°) land right on the axes, making their trigonometric values easy to read off.

confusionCorner.title: Always to the x-axis!
confusionCorner.body: The reference angle is always measured to the [[imp:nearest x-axis]], not the y-axis. This ensures it is an acute angle (less than 90°).

discoveryHook.scenario: Every angle (except quadrantal angles) has an acute 'twin' called its reference angle. This reference angle has the same trigonometric values up to a sign. By finding the reference angle, you can use the exact values you already know for 30°, 45°, and 60° to evaluate trig functions for any angle.

examples.title: Example C — Large Angle

explanation: The [[kw:reference angle]] $ \theta' $ for an angle $ \theta $ is the acute angle formed by the terminal side of $ \theta $ and the horizontal x-axis.
To find $ \theta' $, first determine the quadrant in which the terminal side lies (or the coterminal angle between 0° and 360°).

Quadrant I: $ \theta' = \theta $; Quadrant II: $ \theta' = 180^\circ - \theta $ (or $ \pi - \theta $); Quadrant III: $ \theta' = \theta - 180^\circ $ (or $ \theta - \pi $); Quadrant IV: $ \theta' = 360^\circ - \theta $ (or $ 2\pi - \theta $).
For negative angles or angles > 360°, first find a coterminal angle between 0° and 360° (or 0 and $ 2\pi $).
Reference angles are always between 0° and 90° (0 and $ \frac{\pi}{2} $).

formulaCard.formula: $$ \theta' = \text{acute angle between terminal side and } x\text{-axis} $$

visuals.title: Signs of Trigonometric Functions by Quadrant

explanation: To evaluate a trigonometric function for any angle $ \theta $:
Step 1: Find the reference angle $ \theta' $ (the acute angle with the $ x $-axis).
Step 2: Evaluate the function at $ \theta' $ using known exact values (if special) or a calculator.
Step 3: Determine the sign of the function in the quadrant where $ \theta $ lies.

Signs: In Quadrant I, all are positive. In Quadrant II, only sine and cosecant are positive. In Quadrant III, only tangent and cotangent are positive. In Quadrant IV, only cosine and secant are positive.
The mnemonic '[[kw:All Students Take Calculus]]' reminds you of these signs.

confusionCorner.title: Sign Errors Are Common
confusionCorner.body: The most frequent mistake is forgetting to apply the correct sign. Always determine the quadrant of the [[imp:original angle]] (not the reference angle) to decide the sign. The reference angle only gives the magnitude.

teacherCues: Display the model $ d = \frac{v^2}{32} \sin 2\theta $. Ask: What do the variables represent? How can we use trigonometry to find horizontal distance?
Pose: A golf ball hit at 50° with initial speed 105 ft/s. How far does it travel horizontally?

explanation: [[imp:Understand]]: Identify the given initial speed $ v $ and launch angle $ \theta $. Note that the formula uses $ 2\theta $, so you will need to find the sine of twice the angle.

[[imp:Solve]]: Substitute the values into $ d = \frac{v^2}{32} \sin(2\theta) $. Determine the quadrant of $ 2\theta $ if necessary, find its reference angle, evaluate the sine, and apply the correct sign. Then multiply by $ \frac{v^2}{32} $.
[[imp:Conclude]]: State the horizontal distance in feet, rounded appropriately. Check that the angle is reasonable (between 0° and 90° for a forward launch).

title: Trigonometric Functions of Any Angle
presenterNotes: Emphasize the transition from right-triangle definitions (acute angles) to general definitions using a point on the terminal side. The formula $ r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} $ is key.
For the unit circle, reinforce that $ \sin \theta = y $ and $ \cos \theta = x $ only when $ r = 1 $. Quadrantal angles are a great place to discuss undefined functions due to division by zero.
Reference angles can be tricky. Walk through each quadrant carefully, and stress that the reference angle is always with the x-axis. Use plenty of sketches.
The 'All Students Take Calculus' mnemonic is a student favorite. Have them label the quadrants and practice determining signs before combining with reference angles.
The Blueprint block on projectile motion ties together angle evaluation and a real‑life formula. Point out the $ 2\theta $ in the sine function—a common oversight.
